titleStmt.title: Interview with Joseph E. Goffeney, n.d.
titleStmt.author: Emmet Reed

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph E. Goffeney was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Hello, my name's Joe Goffeney. I'm a veteran of World War II and Korea, but going back to the time when I first considered joining the military was in 1937 or '38. That's a long time ago. My brother proceeded me into the service and that influenced my decision of course to follow in his foot steps. Plus, there were some movies in those days that really glamorized the service; Dick Powell and Ruby Keeler and "Shipmates Stand Together," and all that sort of thing. So, shortly after I graduated from high school I joined the Navy; April 3, 1939, and I went through training at Great Lakes. Training in those days was I think 13 weeks, graduated and went on to San Diego where I attended a Class A school. Then I, upon graduation requested the ship that my brother was on, and that was permissible in those days to allow brothers to serve together. Of course that was rescinded after the Juno tragedy where the five Sullivan brothers were all lost in the same ship sinking. So, on New Year's Eve, 1939, I went a board the USS Case; a mayhem class destroyer. Two months after I went a board the Case my brother was transferred and I stayed on the Case for 62 months (laughter). I finally left the Case on February 1945 that was the only ship that I served on during World War II. When I was relieved from or transferred, I went to a naval air station in the Los Angeles area and I was discharged into the reserve from there. But, some of the questions that were said to me I have trouble relating with because I think they were slanted toward people that were drafted into the military, and these questions, which I reviewed pretty carefully, really didn't apply to me at all. For instance, what my attitude was towards the enemy. I had no attitude toward the enemy until December 7,1941 and my perception changed in about five minutes. On December 7,1941 after a period of training and exercises, we went into Pearl Harbor and went alongside the USS Whitney, a destroyer tender for some routine tender overhaul. Things were beginning to brew a little bit. Although, young sailors,I was 20 years old, we weren't clued in too much at that time into the international politics that was taking place. But, we had an inspection by the commanding officer on December 6, and after the inspection he mustered everybody on the fan-tail, and gave us a little pep talk; and I'll read a portion of what our commanding officer said from a history report that I wrote dealing exclusively with my impressions of the attack and how it effected me. But it--what I wrote here was, "by the commanding officer we were told that our country's relations with Japan were rapidly deteriorating. When at sea, all lookouts were to be constantly on the alert and if and when general quarters sounded, we were to man our battle stations on the double and be prepared to do battle." To quote our commanding officer he said, "it looks like we may have trouble with our little brown brothers." That afternoon the senior officers went a shore and the ship was left in charge of a Reserve Lieutenant and a Reserve Anson. I had the duty and was on watch from four in the morning until eight in the morning on December 7, in the engine room. I was a machinist man. It was what was called a cold-iron watch and all our services such as light and power, water were all being supplied by the tender. We were, in one week, into an overhaul that pretty much incapacitated the ship's ability to fight or to get under way. But, about 7 o'clock in the morning I was relieved for breakfast, came back down to the engine room, made a pot of coffee for the late risers. Being Sunday morning there was a holiday routine. Everybody was sleeping in. A few early risers were on their way to go for a hike in the hills in back of Pearl Harbor, but most of the guys just trickled down to the engine room for that first cup of coffee and cigarette. And while we were sitting around down there we heard a ship along side of us fire its machine guns. Everybody jumped up and their impression was somebody is really going to get into trouble for firing a machine gun in the Harbor. Then there was another burst of machine gun fire and then the crack of a five inch gun. I ran up the hatch and out on the main deck and looked to the stern of the ship just as a Japanese plane flew right over the nest, so close that I could see the pilot looking down on us. If I'd a had a potato or something I could have probably hit the plane, he was that close. But, then I ran to the stern of the ship and I could look at Ford Island and my impression of all the Japanese planes flying around; it was like a swarm of bees. And then about that time, a little bit to the left, there was a tremendous explosion. We couldn't actually see what blew up, but we could see the blast of flame and smoke and felt the shock wave and we presumed that that was an explosion on the Arizona. But, that night our first assignment was to patrol Pearl Harbor all night long. Circling North Island, going past the Arizona, the West Virginia; both of them still burning. On, around, past our sister ship, the Shaw, which was in Voting Dry Dock, and it blew up and resulted in that classic Pearl Harbor attack picture, that tremendous explosion where flames and smoke just obliterated everything. The Shaw was lost, it's entire bow and 25 men I believe, were killed on the Shaw during that explosion. But, we circled around and around and we just couldn't hardly believe what we saw. We--a good friend of mine, after things settled down, and general quarters was secured, we sat up on the deck and tried to come to grips with what we were seeing and it was almost beyond belief. Of course we were physically and emotionally drained, both of us, and we finally decided that the Japanese had really messed up(laughter) and that they would--we'd wipe them from the ocean in a matter of a few months and I have some comments on that. "After things settled down and a steaming watch had been set, a friend and I sat down on the torpedo tubes at the top of the engine room hatch in the cool night air and we tried to collect our thoughts. We were physically and emotionally exhausted and together we pondered the imponderable. As we slowly patrolled past our burning battle ships, our minds rejected what we were seeing. We could not believe that Japan would have the audacity to attack us in our bastion. We finally decided that the Japanese had really messed up and that in a matter of a few months our Navy would wipe the Japanese Fleet from the Pacific. We would later learn that the Japanese Navy was a skilled and deadly adversary and that their weaponry was equal, and in some cases superior to ours. Of course two young sailors had no way of knowing that Japan's primary objective was to force a negotiated peace to secure their dominance in China and southeast Asia." But, we left, we fueled ship, left Pearl Harbor about noon on the 8th and assumed our patrol position off of Diamondhead, and for about a week we patrolled in circles, and I submarine patrolled. It seemed interminable. We had no idea what was going on. Finally, we saw the fighting tops of three battle ships coming out of Pearl Harbor. They were the only three battle ships left that were able to get under way, and with other destroyers we formed a screen and set a course for the West Coast. And we--sometime between Christmas and New Year's, we arrived with the Maryland and the Tennessee, I believe at Bremerton Navy Yard. And the other battleship went to San Francisco, Hunter's Point Navy Yard. But, that was how the war started for the ship that I was on. But, some of the--the Case was a lucky ship. I've written a history of the ship and going back a little bit; it was a third class of the so-called modern destroyers. The Case hull number was the 370, and it was, as I said, the third of a class of destroyers, after the old four-pipe destroyers that were built in World War I. The Case went into commission in 1936, so it had a few miles on it when the war started. But, as a credit to her engineering crew and to the people that built the ship and the people that designed the ship; never once in the entire war was the Case, or did the Case fail to meet a deployment do to an engineering breakdown. Only one time we failed to show up on time. We came up from Guatal Canal and we went along side a tender, the USS Dixie, in the New Hebrides. Everybody ran across the gangway to get some ice cream 'cause the tender had a big Gee duct(phonetic) stand. Well in about a couple hours the crew started dropping like flies and it turned out that the ice cream had botchilism or something. But, there were so many people down that the ship, from the captain right on down, that they were unable to get on their way. Our ship's doctor, he performed admirably, but he carried his own bucket with him and--to throw up in, you know. So--but that was the only time that the Case failed to make a deployment. Case only lost three people during the war. None do to hostile action. They were washed over the side in extremely rough weather. So, I consider myself very fortunate, not only to have served on a ship like the Case, but for the relationships that we maintain 60 years later with some of the crew. The Case, I guess for the past 15 years has had a reunion and we're having one in September this year. I think it'll be our 16th. But, we have a reunion in a different place every year. We've been to San Diego twice; we've been to Reno twice; we've been to Norfolk; Portland, Maine; Saint Louis. We try to accommodate the few of us that are left. We're scattered all over the country so we try to accommodate everybody's travel needs. But, our numbers are getting fewer and fewer. Our first reunion we had maybe 40 or 50 men and their wives, and now we have almost as many widows as we do survivors(laughter). And, these gals are very faithful. They show up just about every union. Unfortunately, we haven't been able to attend all of, them, but the next one is going to be in Colorado Springs and God willing my wife and I--my wife by the way, has been my helpmate, friend, lover for 60 years (laughter). We got married October 26, 1941. Ship had come back from Hawaii for a month; a month leave and recreation, and we got married in Yuma and old Pastor Brown must have said the right words because we're still there (laughter).

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Let me ask you Joe, where--after--when you escorted the two battleships back to the states, and I guess it was what, the latter part of '41 or the early part of '42?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: It was between Christmas and New Year's when we arrived.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Where did the Case--well let me just make this assumption, you were on the Case for over five years?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: 52--62 months.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: I guess my question is, you were on her almost for the entire war weren't you?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Now, let me ask you a question. If you would relate to us some of the things, the areas that the Case went into after you came back to combat zone?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: If you would relate some of those battles--areas that you were in and?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Okay. Well, the first few months we were on what was called the Pineapple Run and the military--the Navy, I guess, they scraped together just about anything that would float to start shipping supplies to the forward area. We saw whole lumbar packets, little things. In fact, one of the ships that we escorted across was called the Lumbar Lady. It got lost everyday and we'd have to go find it. There were great lake oar boats. Anything that would float. So, we escorted these convoys back and forth until May of 1942, and then the Midway Battle was in the wind. So, we made a quick run to the States, spent eight hours, and got four hours liberty and peace(laughter)in San Francisco. Alice had an apartment there and I got to see her for 4 hours, but anyway. Then we rushed back to Pearl Harbor, we took on a bunch of Marine Raiders at Pearl, went to Midway; this was just a few days prior to the attack, dropped the Marines off and then continued on to Kodiac, Alaska. And, we were in the Aleutians at--near Dutch Harbor when the Japanese made their fate with the aircraft carrier bombing Pearl Harbor or Dutch Harbor on a couple of occasions. And, we were hiding in the fog (laughter) because there was only about three destroyers up there. Fortunately, they didn't find us, but as our strength grew we escorted the ships that occupied Haydack(phonetic) and on two occasions we bombarded Kiska which the Japanese had occupied. And, we're credited with sinking a couple of ships that were in Kiska Harbor at the time of our attack. As an aside, when the war started the Navy was ill-prepared to supply ships in remote places. They had two supply ships and one refrigeration ship. So, we were living on, at times, on literally on hard tack, but wherever we were able to drop the hook we literally dropped more than the ship's hook. Every hook that was available went over the side and we caught, many times enough fresh fish to feed the crew, and we depended on it until we were finally able to get some supplies. We were up there for more than six months and it was tough, tough duty. Some of the roughest ocean water in the world is up in the Aleutian Islands. Miserable, miserable weather. So, in October we got orders to Pearl Harbor. We went from Pearl, escorting a convoy back to Mare Island Navy Yard, a quick overhaul and then back to Pearl and then we joined a task force and went down to Guatal Canal. By that time we were very much aware of what was going on down there, and what a bloody battle ground that turned out to be. However, we were fortunate. We came in contact with a Japanese task force only one time, but we managed to duck into a rainsquall and avoided combat because all that was there was our ship, a New Zealand gun boat and one other small patrol craft, and the Japanese had a couple of light cruisers and about a dozen destroyers; and what they were doing was dropping off supplies in big, rubberized pouchs so that the--hopefully the Japanese would pick them up and pull them a shore. But, we snagged several of them the next morning and there was souvenirs for everybody. It was food, medical supplies and things like that. We also did some bombardment in support of the Marines that were there. And, when that settled down a little bit then we went into service with the USS Saratoga, one of our prewar aircraft carriers, and we operated with her for about six months. And--but I do have, well I don't have it with me, but the Case was awarded seven battle stars for service; all in the Pacific. Starting with Pearl Harbor and then there was the Marshall Island assault; there was Guatal Canal campaign. We operated off of New Guinea. The assault on Truk, big Japanese base, Truk. Yap, the Philippine invasion; we were supporting that. We were with Admiral McCain, that's John McCain's father. He was the task force commander of the task group that we were with, but the latter part of the war we escorted carriers more than anything. We--the Sypan Turkey shoot when they about eliminated the Japanese Naval Air Force, why we were right in the middle of that. Every night Japanese bombers would come in, flying low across the water trying to penetrate the screen to get into the air craft carriers. Often times we shot up our own ships, unfortunately. Our gunners, other people's gunners would zero in on a ship, or on a plane and wouldn't let up as he was flying through the task group, and if another ship happened to be on the other side--why, and unfortunately we lost some men from our own fire. But, then we picked up a couple of Japanese pilots that were floating around (laughter). That was interesting we--we had him--he'd been in the water about a week, he was in bad shape, but we nursed him back to health and treated his saltwater ulcers, which are ugly things, and then finely transferred him to an aircraft carrier. We rendezvoused with a couple of submarines that had torpedoed a Japanese transport that was transporting British prisoners of war back to Japan, and the sub sank the transport and didn't know what to do with these people. They took them a board, but they were severely--there was almost 200 of them. About a hundred on each sub, and they were going to transfer them to our ship, but when we got to the rendezvous point it was too rough. So, we transferred our medical people and supplies, blankets and so on to the submarines and they proceeded on. And then, probably our next and probably the most interesting part, cause allot of this stuff was very, very boring. Day after day, after day of just steaming. We became part of the bombardment group making the preinvasion bombardments of Iwo Jima. And, we ran up there four or five times. The last trip up we scared off a Japanese destroyer; and another ship and the Case chased this destroyer full power north towards other bases that they had north of Iwo Jima engaged in a service action and sank the Japanese destroyer. We were confused or confounded by the number of people that were floating in the water. We found out later that they had a thousand Japanese troops on that destroyer and they were in the process of taking them to Iwo Jima when we surprised them and then gave chase and sank the thing. Our gun crew scored the initial hit on the--at 14 1/2 thousand yards they scored a hit midship, at the water line and it slowed the Japanese destroyer to about fifteen knots, and we closed in real quickly, and sank the thing. Before it did, and I want to make mention of this, there was a--well everybody was riveted, their eyes were riveted on the ship and our shells hitting the ship. There was one sea men that was supposed to be a lookout. He was stationed on the wing of the bridge and his duty was to observe the sea, and the air, and the area around the ship and he spotted torpedo winks. And, the ship turned and torpedo went down. Some people say it bounced off the side of the ship, I don't know, but it was close enough that you could see the wink just a few feet on one side of the ship and then the second torpedo on the other side of the ship. The fact that this sea men was doing his job in spite of the distractions saved the ship. It would of--we would have been hit twice and sunk undoubtedly, so. But anyway, after that I left the ship, but I remember flying over it. I managed to get air transportation from Sypan, that's where I left the ship; managed to get air transport to Pearl Harbor and I looked down at the ship and it was kind of sad. This had been my home and a good home for more than five years, and I looked down at it and I felt a kind of a lump in my throat. But anyway, that just about concludes my story. I could go into allot of detail on other things it would probably be boring.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well Joe, we appreciate your coming in and telling us. It's very interesting. I--of course I being a third year Navy man myself was hanging on to every word because, although I wasn't old enough to get into World War II--but all of those things you were talking on the DD, I served the ward five DD's in my career.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Five DDs?

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Five DD's, and I know exactly what you're taking about. The first DD I was ever on they had to almost pry me loose. I was on their for four years and they said you're gonna to have to go, you know; and I almost cried too when I left that ship. I was on there so long Joe and you probably got--had the same feeling, is that a person stays a board that long, they get to thinking that they own that ship. That that ship is their personal property, you know. But, I love that ship and I love those DDs.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Well, I went from fireman, third class and they had--that was just one step above an apprentice seaman to the senior chief machinist mate on that thing and called the Tojo chief, if it hadn't a been for Tojo I wouldn't have made chief.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well, Joe were you--how many years total did you have in?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: I beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: How many years total did you have in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Well, about 6 1/2 there, but then I went in the reserve, got called back in during the Korean War and went right back a board another destroyer and went on to on Japan?

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: The course destroyers in Korea and also in Vietnam, their main duties there was shore bombardment and escorting aircraft carriers, and I would imagine your--you say you picked up another destroyer for Korea when you came back in or?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Yeah, when I came back in, yeah. The Herbert J. Thomas hull number was 833 it was a radar picket.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: I know it well. I wouldn't have know it, but I know Herbert Thomas.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Goffeney
sp.p: Well, it's been a pleasure talking to you guys (laughter) I did all the talking.
